title: Pleasure, danger, escape
hook: the gratification, the danger and the way out of sense pleasure (MN 13)
carry: the escape is from the hook

segments.voice: Yesterday: sihanada, the lion's roar, a claim made from sure ground. Your line: a lion's roar.

Every app store page has the same layout. What it does. The screenshots. Five-star reviews from people who love it. Almost none has a section called: what this will cost you. And none has a third: how to stop using it when you want to. MN 13 asks for all three, about sense pleasure. Not to ruin the pleasure. To see the whole of it, plainly, before deciding.
screen: `WHAT IT DOES.` → `WHAT IT COSTS.` → `HOW TO STOP.`

segments.voice: MN 13, the Greater Discourse on the Mass of Suffering, looks at sense pleasure three ways. In Pali: assada, adinava, nissarana. The gratification, the danger, the escape. Gratification first, and the Buddha doesn't deny it. The pleasure and joy that arise from the five cords of sense pleasure, sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches, are real. Then the danger. A person earns a living by a trade: counting, accounting, farming, trading, herding, archery, service to the king. They face cold and heat, gadflies and mosquitoes, hunger and thirst. If the work fails, they grieve: all my effort was for nothing. If it succeeds, they worry: kings, thieves, fire or flood could take it, or an heir could squander it. And the larger danger: for the sake of pleasures, kings quarrel with kings, nobles with nobles, householders with householders; mother with son, son with mother, brother with sister, friend with friend. Then the escape: the removal of desire and lust for sense pleasures. Not the removal of every joy. In MN 36, the Buddha says he came to see that the joy of deep meditation wasn't something to fear. The escape is from the hook, not from happiness. The sutta says anyone who doesn't see gratification as gratification, danger as danger and escape as escape can't fully understand sense pleasures, let alone guide someone else. And he applies the same three to the body and to feelings.
screen: `ASSADA — THE GRATIFICATION.` · `ADINAVA — THE DANGER.` · `NISSARANA — THE ESCAPE.` · `ALL THREE, OR YOU'RE HOOKED.` · then, large: `PLEASURE, DANGER, ESCAPE.`

segments.voice: Think of one pleasure you love, coffee, a show, a certain food, and give it its due: notice the real enjoyment in it, even in memory. Then name its cost plainly, without shame, in time, money, sleep or peace. Last, touch the third lightly: what would it be like to enjoy it without needing it? Nothing has to be given up; just see all three.
Pleasure. In MN 13, sense pleasure is seen three ways: its gratification, its danger, and the way out.
Your line: the escape is from the hook. The joy itself can stay. Day four hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the triad of gratification, danger and escape as a way of reflecting on desires; the lay precepts ask for restraint in sense pleasures rather than renouncing them.

fork.setup: a person's business succeeds. in MN 13, what comes with the success?
options: worry that kings, thieves, fire or flood will take it
fork.reveal: success brings its own danger: guarding what you have. the sutta follows pleasure all the way to quarrels between families and kings.

original.note: Pali nissaraṇa: escape, the way out; the third of the triad.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says pleasure is bad.
what it means: see a pleasure whole: its gratification, its danger, and the way out of being hooked.
what a scholar hears: assāda, ādīnava, nissaraṇa is a recurring triad in the suttas; MN 13 applies it to sense pleasures, bodily form and feelings in turn.
recall: a lute: effort tuned to an even pitch

chat.says: Does Buddhism say that enjoying things is bad?
options: MN 13 calls the gratification real, then asks you to see the danger and the way out.
Yes, every enjoyment is a trap, so the goal is to feel no joy at all.
No, the more pleasure you chase, the closer you get to awakening.
chat.meaning: MN 13 sees sense pleasure three ways: the gratification, which is real, the danger, and the escape, which is from the hook, not from joy.
